Jude Bellingham's game-changing display against PSV in Madrid, on November 24, 2026, was hailed by Real Madrid head coach Jose Mourinho [Manu Fernandez/AP Photo]By AFP and ReutersPublished On 25 Nov 202625 Nov 2026
Real Madrid star Jude Bellingham has brushed aside comparisons with football great Zinedine Zidane following his sensational goal against PSV in the Champions League.
The England international came on at half-time with Los Blancos trailing and inspired a sensational second-half display, including a magnificent effort from distance, at the Santiago Bernabeu on Tuesday.
Bellingham said he “did not know” how he scored his brilliant goal, flicking the ball up on the edge of the box and slicing a stunning effort inside the far post.
Having seen an acrobatic volley blocked minutes earlier, the England midfielder controlled Kylian Mbappe’s pass with two touches in the air and curled a superb shot into ⁠⁠the far corner from well outside the area.
“I have no idea what I did,” Bellingham told RMTV. “I had the ball in a good position and thought about shooting.”
The 23-year-old, upon joining Real Madrid, took Zidane’s number five shirt in “homage” to the Frenchman, whom he admired, and some have compared his goal to a Zidane-style strike.
“I do things that you guys think are similar to Zidane, but he was much better than me,” Bellingham told reporters.
Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho hailed Bellingham’s game-changing display as the midfielder gave Mourinho credit for helping him find arguably the best form he has enjoyed at Madrid in recent weeks, with Los Blancos winning a 10th straight match, but the coach said the midfielder only had himself to thank.

The funeral of Muhammad Majid Abu al-Awf and his family [Mahmoud Issa/Reuters]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 25 Nov 202625 Nov 2026
An Israeli air attack on Gaza has killed a senior Palestinian security official and his wife and daughters, according to a statement from the enclave’s Ministry of Interior.
In a statement posted on its Telegram channel on Wednesday, the ministry identified the official as Muhammad Majid Abu al-Awf, 47, director of the Internal Security Service in northern Gaza.

Noura Ezzat Abual-Awf, his wife, aged 41, and his children, Yusra Mohammed Abu al-Awf, 15, and Jana Mohammed Abu al-Awf, 13, were also killed in the strike, the statement added.
The ministry described the killings as a “horrific massacre perpetrated by the Israeli occupation forces when they bombed [the family’s] residence in the Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, at dawn today”.
The attack is part of “ongoing attempts to undermine the security apparatus in the Gaza Strip in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society”, it added.
The strike comes less than 24 hours after the killing of the Internal Security Service’s director general, Brigadier-General Naim Abu Nahal.
Israeli attacks continue
Israeli strikes reported overnight killed several people, according to medical sources.

The Chinese Communist Party has launched investigations into the party’s Shanghai secretary Chen Jining for alleged “serious violations of discipline and law” – usually code for corruption.
The anticorruption watchdog, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, announced the probe in a brief statement on Tuesday, according to Xinhua News Agency, but did not give more details.

It comes amid widespread purges in the Political Bureau, one of the top bodies of the CCP, as the party prepares for its next congress in the second half of 2027, where President Xi Jinping is expected to clinch his fourth five-year term.
Xi, who has pushed greater party discipline and anticorruption, has for years pursued a long, intense purge on a scale not seen since the rule of Mao Zedong, experts say.
Chen is the fourth high-ranking Politburo member to be pushed out in two years.

From left: Politics student Syed Ali, Haanyah Cassam, who is training to be a teacher and law student Aayan Hashmi say they have experienced discrimination at their universities (Photos courtesy of Ali, Cassam and Hashmi)By Sunniya Ahmad PirzadaPublished On 25 Nov 202625 Nov 2026
London, United Kingdom – Haanyah Cassam, 23, was only a few weeks into her first year at the University of London’s School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS) when a security guard walked into a hall where she and other students had gathered for a lecture.
Most of the group were Muslim.

According to Cassam, the guard told them they were behaving “like a pack of animals, especially those hijabis”. He then made a remark about “towel heads” and walked off.
Cassam, who chose to wear the hijab despite her family’s fears for her safety, told Al Jazeera, “It takes a lot of confidence and a lot of power to put something on your head that you know is going to make you a target.”
At the time, she felt “there was no one we could go to about this”, she said.
She later raised the issue with a professor, and was told their hands were tied by bureaucracy. The guard left the university at the end of that year.
